paragraphs.heading: What it was
paragraphs.text: The Industrial Revolution was a period when the world economy moved toward manufacturing that was more widespread, efficient and stable. It followed the Second Agricultural Revolution and is sometimes called the First Industrial Revolution, to set it apart from the second one that came after it. It began in Great Britain around 1760 and had reached continental Europe and the United States by about 1840. At its heart was a move from making things by hand to making them with machines, along with new methods for chemicals and iron, more use of water and steam power, machine tools, and the mechanised factory.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: Economic historians agree that its start is the most important event in human history for material progress, rivalled only by the adoption of farming. Output soared, and population grew as never before. It reached into almost every part of life: average income and population began a long, steady rise, and living standards improved for most people in the Western world, though some argue real gains only came in the 20th century. It also shifted where things were made, from China and India before it to North America and Western Europe after it.

paragraphs.heading: Britain and cloth
paragraphs.text: Britain led the way. By the middle of the 1700s it was the leading commercial nation, with output per person, or GDP per capita, well above the world average, and many of the new inventions were British. Textiles were the first industry to use modern production methods and became the biggest by jobs, value of output and money invested. Britain took up machine spinning quickly in the 1780s, and the method spread to continental Europe and the US early in the next century. After 1800 steam power and iron production grew fast.

paragraphs.heading: How much faster
paragraphs.text: The gains were huge. Machine spinning of cotton, driven first by water and later by steam, raised output per worker about 500 times, the power loom raised it 40 times, and the cotton gin made pulling seeds out of cotton 50 times more productive. Steam engines grew efficient enough to burn only a fifth to a tenth as much fuel. Once stationary engines could drive rotary motion they suited factories, and the high-pressure engine, strong for its weight, suited transport.

paragraphs.heading: Iron and machine tools
paragraphs.text: Making iron changed too. Using coke in place of charcoal cut the fuel cost of making iron and allowed bigger blast furnaces, with the savings that come from working at scale. Puddling made structural iron more cheaply than the older finery forge, the rolling mill worked fifteen times faster than hammering, and hot blast, developed in 1828, greatly raised fuel efficiency. Meanwhile the first machine tools appeared: the screw-cutting lathe, the milling machine and the cylinder boring machine. They made precision metal parts affordable to produce, although interchangeable parts took decades more to master.

paragraphs.heading: Naming it
paragraphs.text: The name has its own story. Its earliest recorded use was in 1799, when the French envoy Louis-Guillaume Otto announced that France had joined the race to industrialise. Friedrich Engels used the phrase in 1844, and Arnold Toynbee's lectures of 1881 are credited with making it popular. Historians still argue about when it began and ended and how fast things changed, and some, such as John Clapham and Nicholas Crafts, say the change was gradual and that revolution is the wrong word.
